title: NIPUN Bharat and the 2024 foundational-learning recovery
summary: The National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy was launched under NEP 2020 on 5 July 2021, targeting foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by the end of Grade 2 by 2026-27. ASER 2024 recorded the largest foundational gains in the survey's twenty years: Standard III government-school reading rose from 16.3 per cent (2022) to 23.4, above its 2018 level of 20.9, and Standard III arithmetic reached 33.7 per cent nationally, the highest in over a decade. Reading did not recover to 2018 at any grade.
claimAtLaunch: Universal foundational literacy and numeracy by the end of Grade 2, for every child, by 2026-27.
whatHappened: Arithmetic in 2024 exceeded the 2018 level at every grade; reading recovered to 2018 at no grade. Standard III reading went 27.3 (2018) to 20.5 (2022) to 27.1 (2024); Standard V reading 50.5 to 42.8 to 48.8; Standard III arithmetic 28.2 to 25.9 to 33.7. Holding sector weights fixed at their 2018 values, the composition-neutral 2018-to-2024 changes are +0.0 for Standard III reading, -1.3 for Standard V reading, +5.8 for Standard III subtraction and +3.3 for Standard V division. In March 2025 the Rajya Sabha Standing Committee recorded that 'despite the progress recorded, this is a target that we are highly unlikely to meet' and recommended extending the deadline from 2027 to 2032. It also recorded that the mission 'has been re-focused recently to exclude oral reading fluency as one of its objective', because oral reading fluency was a Grade 3 target and Grade 3 falls outside NEP's five-year foundational stage - and recommended that it be put back.
caseFor: The gains are large, national and near-universal: every state recovered in Standard III government-school reading, and Standard III arithmetic rose in every major state except three. They are concentrated exactly where the mission operates - Standards I to III - and Standard VIII arithmetic, which the mission does not touch, is flat across the whole window at 44.1, 44.7, 45.8, which is what rules out a general instrument drift or enumerator effect. They are concentrated in government schools, where the policy operates, and composition cannot explain the government-school gain because it is a within-sector figure: for Standard III government reading to have risen from 16.3 to 23.4 compositionally, the children who left would need negative proficiency. The delivery chain was independently observed rather than self-reported: ASER's own surveyors, in 15,728 government schools, found more than 80 per cent had received an FLN directive, 77.6 per cent had a teacher trained in person, 74.5 per cent had received teaching-learning material and more than 95 per cent had distributed textbooks - the rare case where the MIS-standing-in-for-outcome problem does not bite. Standard III arithmetic at 33.7 is the highest in over a decade and Standard V division at 30.7 is above every reading in the 2012-2022 span: not a return to trend but above it. And the independent instrument's own director credits the policy: 'We have not seen improvements of this magnitude in the last 20 years. Everything seems to point towards NEP 2020 and its focus on foundational skills. It is the first time that there has been a systemic national push to improve foundational learning outcomes.'
caseAgainst: On reading the country did not recover at all. After six years, two of them with a foundational mission and a National Education Policy, rural India's Standard III children read no better than in 2018 and slightly worse - 27.1 against 27.3, and composition-adjusted +0.0. And 2018 was itself a weak level: Standard V reading in 2018 (50.5) was below 2010 (53.7) and Standard III arithmetic in 2018 (28.2) was 8.1 points below 2010, so 'recovery to 2018' means recovery to a level below where the country stood at the start of the UPA's second term. Roughly three of four Standard III children still cannot read a Standard II text and two of three still cannot subtract. There is no causal identification and nobody claims one: the mission launched nationally and simultaneously, with no untreated comparison group, no staggered adoption and no discontinuity, and the FLN implementation questions were asked for the first time in 2024, so no difference-in-differences of any kind is possible. The 2022 baseline is already partially recovered, which inflates the measured gain - ASER's own state surveys in Karnataka, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal during 2021 found learning had fallen far further than the 2018-to-2022 gap suggests and that 'there had been a recovery between 2021 and 2022', before the mission could plausibly have bitten. A large policy-independent confounder is uncontrolled: maternal illiteracy fell 13 points and mothers educated past Standard X nearly doubled between 2018 and 2024, which would raise early reading with or without the mission - and that makes the flatness of reading look worse, not better. ASER's own classroom fieldwork, in the same report, finds the mission's pedagogy largely is not happening: across 45 lessons in 24 Standard II classrooms, students were observed using any teaching-learning material other than textbooks in six snapshots, small-group activities in one classroom, and independent writing in none, while teachers reported that documenting student-level outcomes had displaced teaching time. Inputs moved the wrong way year on year - teachers trained in person 80.4 to 77.6 per cent, funds received for FLN activities 43.6 to 36.2 - while outputs rose. And a uniform national intervention produced radically non-uniform results: Standard III government-school reading spans over 40 points, from Himachal Pradesh at 49.7 to Telangana at 6.8, which is weak evidence for the intervention - with the single largest gain in Uttar Pradesh, which is also the state driving the national attendance gain.
shockExposure: The measurement window straddles the COVID closures entirely. There was no field ASER between November 2018 and November 2022, so the pre-period is four years before the mission launched and the trough was never measured. Any attribution rests on two points either side of a shock whose depth is unmeasured.

title: India's school closures, 2020-2022
summary: Indian schools were never classified fully open for 707 consecutive days, from 25 March 2020 to 1 March 2022 - 47 days fully open in the entire 25-month window. On UNESCO's own definition of closure duration, which counts fully closed and partially open days together, India's 93 weeks is the unique global maximum across 210 countries, against a global mean of 40.6. On full closure alone India's 25 weeks ranks 58th. The affected population, 294,893,120 children, is the largest of any country in the world.
whatHappened: Closure was state-decided and grade-differentiated. India spent 173 days fully closed and 476 days - 61 per cent of the window - in UNESCO's single undifferentiated 'partially open' bucket, which covers everything from one grade in one state shut to all primary grades shut across most of the country. That grade-differentiation is what reconciles the mild national label with ASER's stronger claim that 'primary schools were closed for almost two years': for most of the partially open days senior grades had reopened while primary had not - and primary is where the learning loss landed. Measured at the end, Standard III reading had fallen 6.8 points and Standard V reading 7.7, against arithmetic losses of 2.3 points; government-school enrolment among rural 6-14s rose 7.3 points and then fell 6.1 back out by 2024.
caseFor: Closure decisions were taken by state governments during a pandemic that killed an officially acknowledged number of Indians in the hundreds of thousands, in a country with the world's largest school-age population, extreme classroom density and a health system that came visibly close to collapse in April-May 2021. Comparators with far greater resources made similar or harder choices - the Philippines 75 weeks fully closed, Uganda 66, Bangladesh 63, against India's 25 - and India's ranking is 58th on full closure precisely because it reopened in stages rather than keeping everything shut. Grade-differentiated reopening, which is what drives the 93-week figure, is a more discriminating policy than a blanket rule, not a worse one: it kept senior grades running through examinations while the youngest and least vaccinated stayed home. The measured learning loss, when it was finally taken, was smaller in arithmetic than expected and was substantially recovered within two years.
caseAgainst: On the measure UNESCO itself uses, India kept its schools shut longer than any of the 210 countries it tracked, for the largest child population in the world, and 61 per cent of that duration sits in a bucket so coarse that the state of Indian schooling for 476 days cannot be reconstructed from any published source, Indian or international. The federal division that produced grade-differentiation also produced the measurement gap: neither UNESCO nor the Government of India published a state-by-state or grade-by-grade closure-duration series, and no Indian government document stating a national closure duration was retrieved at all. Most damningly, India did not measure learning during its own closures. There was no field ASER between November 2018 and November 2022 - the 2020 and 2021 rounds were telephone surveys with no learning assessment - and no government instrument filled the gap, so the depth of the trough is unrecoverable in principle. A country that closed its schools longer than any other chose not to find out what that did to children while it was doing it, and then measured only at the end, four years after the last pre-COVID reading.
shockExposure: The pandemic itself is the shock; this record is about the response to it and its measurement, not about the disease. Note that the record is typed as an episode rather than a shock precisely because closure duration in India was a sequence of state decisions rather than an external event.

title: The Ministry of Education's two framings of ASER 2024, six months apart
summary: On 4 February 2025 the Ministry of Education issued a factsheet on ASER 2024 headlined 'Leap in Rural School Enrollment' which reproduced ASER's findings near-verbatim while deleting every 2022 data point. On 28 July 2025 the same Ministry published a backgrounder attributing the learning recovery to its own policies - and reinstated the same 2022 troughs, because the recovery cannot be shown without them.
whatHappened: Three separate 2022 figures were removed from the February document. ASER: government enrolment among 6-14s 'was 65.6 per cent in 2018. The pandemic saw large increases in government school enrollments (72.9 per cent in 2022). But by 2024, the all-India figure declined to 66.8 per cent.' The factsheet: '...In 2018, 65.5 per cent... By 2024, the all-India figure increased to 66.8 per cent.' A 6.1-point decline from the 2022 peak was presented, under a headline claiming a leap, as an increase - by deleting the peak. Standard III government reading lost its 'fell to 16.3 per cent in 2022'; Standard III arithmetic lost its '25.9 per cent in 2022'; and 'dropped from 13.1 per cent in 2018 to 7.5 per cent in 2022, but stayed about the same at 7.9 per cent in 2024' became 'dropped sharply from 13.1 per cent in 2018 to 7.9 per cent in 2024'. In July, the backgrounder - sourced internally to the Department's own Ready Reckoner - wrote that Class III government-school reading reached 23.4 per cent in 2024, 'up from 16.3 per cent in 2022 and 20.9 per cent in 2018', and that arithmetic reached 27.6 per cent 'compared to 20.2 per cent in 2022'.
caseFor: A press factsheet is a summary, not a statistical publication, and summarising a six-year movement from 2018 to 2024 without narrating the intermediate trough is ordinary précis rather than misrepresentation. The underlying ASER report was public, in full, on the same day; nothing was concealed from anyone who read it. The figures reproduced are accurate as far as they go, the endpoints are correctly stated, and the enrolment claim is defensible on its own terms: rural government-school enrolment in 2024 IS higher than in 2018. And when the Ministry did make an attribution claim, in July, it stated the trough plainly and correctly.
caseAgainst: The February document is not a summary. It reproduces ASER's own sentences near-verbatim and then removes three numbers, each of which is the one that makes the sentence say the opposite of what the headline claims. The headline is 'Leap in Rural School Enrollment' and the underlying movement it describes is a 6.1-point fall from a peak - a leap manufactured by deleting the peak. The out-of-school figure is the clearest case: ASER's own sentence records that the fall stopped in 2022 and the number ticked back up, and the factsheet turns it into a sharp drop by removing the stop. And the July document settles the question of whether the deletions were incidental: the same Ministry, on the same data, reinstated exactly those figures six months later, because the recovery story needs the trough that the enrolment story needed gone. Same ministry, opposite framings, identical underlying data.

title: UDISE+ moves to individual student records and 1.7 crore enrolments disappear
summary: From reference year 2022-23 the school statistics system replaced school-wise consolidated returns with individual student records carrying a unique educational ID and voluntary Aadhaar, to weed out duplicate and ghost entries. Total enrolment fell from 26.52 crore (FY2021-22) to 24.80 crore (FY2023-24), a fall of 1.72 crore. No back-cast, no dual-basis year and no reconciliation exists, so how much of the fall is deduplication and how much is real decline has never been published.
claimAtLaunch: Accurate tracking of dropouts, and savings to government through 'precise identification of beneficiaries for benefit transfers of Samagra Shiksha scheme, PM POSHAN Scheme, National Scholarship scheme etc.'
whatHappened: The Ministry disclosed the break, in its own disclaimer, naming GER, NER and dropout rate as not strictly comparable - and never naming pupil-teacher ratio, the one headline indicator whose numerator is the raw re-based enrolment count. In the same breath it disclosed that the denominator moved too: population projections were 'moderated' by the Ministry itself using SRS birth-rate trends, UIDAI Aadhaar-saturation reports and the trends of adjoining states, putting Aadhaar on both sides of the GER ratio. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 reports were released together at end-December 2024, so the break-year datum entered the public record already paired with a successor. A second structural break followed in 2025-26, reclassifying everything onto NEP's 5+3+3+4 stages with a back-cast whose restated values contradict those originally published for the same years - secondary GER 66.5 against 77.4 for FY2023-24.
caseFor: Deduplication is a real improvement and its direction is knowable: it can only remove records, never add them, so the pre-2022 counts were inflated and the new ones are closer to the truth. A system with a unique identifier per child is the precondition for tracking a dropout at all, which school-wise aggregates cannot do by construction, and it removes the incentive for a school to carry a child on its rolls for a mid-day meal or a scholarship it does not deliver. The break was disclosed rather than buried: the Ministry published an explicit incomparability statement, named the affected indicators, stated that the projections had been moderated, and told users the two series may not be joined. Aadhaar seeding reached about 90 per cent by 2025-26, so the correction is largely complete and the post-2022-23 series is internally consistent going forward.
caseAgainst: The one number that would let anyone read the reform - how much of 1.72 crore was ghosts and how much was children - has never been published, and the Ministry holds both bases and could produce a dual run for a single year. Without it, every longitudinal claim about Indian school enrolment since 2021 is unresolvable in either direction. The intensity of the correction maps administrative capacity rather than schooling: Aadhaar seeding ran from 24.2 per cent in Meghalaya to 98.1 in Andhra Pradesh, so the measured fall is larger where Aadhaar penetration is higher, which has nothing to do with children. The fall is concentrated in primary - 14.4 per cent in Classes I-V in two years against a flat higher secondary - and a pure-deduplication story has to explain that concentration, which the Ministry has never evidenced. The disclosure was constructed after the fact: the 2022-23 report carries the incomparability language in a weaker form with no bridge sentence and no mention of the projection moderation, and the claim that '2022-23 and 2023-24 are comparable' appears only retrospectively, in the document that benefited from having a comparator. That claim is also wrong for dropout, on the Ministry's own published definition: dropout differences year t against year t+1, so the FY2022-23 rate counted the removed records as children who stopped being enrolled - primary dropout reads 1.45, then 7.8, then 1.9, then 0.3, and a single-year spike that vanishes is not a behavioural event. Finally the presentation omits the number entirely: the PIB release for UDISE+ 2025-26 reports teachers, PTR, dropout, retention, GER, transition, single-teacher and zero-enrolment schools, computers, internet, electricity, toilets and female representation - every one framed as an improvement - and contains no total enrolment figure at all.

title: A national teacher-vacancy statistic, tabled for a decade and then withdrawn
summary: From 2014 the Ministry routinely tabled all-India totals for sanctioned, in-position and vacant school teaching posts in both Houses, drawn from Annual Work Plan and Budget and Project Approval Board returns. The last full national figure was given on 02.08.2023 (Rajya Sabha Unstarred 1460); the last vacancy-only national figure on 07.02.2024 (Rajya Sabha Unstarred 525). Since then no answer in either House has carried a sanctioned or a vacancy number at any level. The Ministry continues to compute it: it furnished 63,26,207 sanctioned and 9,59,148 vacant for 2023-24, and 69,85,760 and 9,82,662 for 2024-25, to the Standing Committee on 7 January 2025, printed in the 368th Report of 08.08.2025.
whatHappened: The refusal formulation - that education is in the Concurrent List and the data is maintained by States - appears in 1 of 46 retrieved answers from the 16th Lok Sabha and in 37 of about 76 from the 17th and 18th, and its spread maps onto the disappearance of the tables. The source migrated with it: AWP&B and PAB minutes (2015-2019), which carry sanctioned posts, then PRABANDH (2020-2024), then UDISE+ (2025-2026), which does not. A full-text search of the UDISE+ 2023-24 and 2024-25 national reports returns zero occurrences of any form of "vacancy" or "sanction"; UDISE+ holds no sanctioned-post denominator, so no vacancy is computable from it. On 17.12.2025 an MP put the Ministry’s own two Standing Committee totals to the Minister by number and asked him to confirm them (Rajya Sabha Starred 193); the reply neither confirmed nor denied and contained no figure. On 20.07.2026 a question asking for state-wise and level-wise sanctioned and vacant posts (Lok Sabha Unstarred 87) was answered with teachers in position only.
caseFor: The constitutional position is real and is not a pretext. Education is in the Concurrent List, recruitment and service conditions are state functions, and the Union directly administers about 3,000 of roughly 14.7 lakh schools - about 0.2 per cent. A sanctioned post is created by a state government under state rules, so there is no national definition of sanctioned strength and no national sanctioning authority. The aggregates that were tabled show exactly the defects that argument predicts: "vacant" is an arithmetic residual rather than an observation; the 2023-24 national total silently drops Tamil Nadu, which did not report on PRABANDH; and several annexures build a TOTAL row over 27, 28 or 30 of 36 jurisdictions without saying so. Migrating parliamentary answers to UDISE+ moves them onto a census-based instrument with a published methodology, and answering with teachers in position - a quantity actually collected - rather than a residual assembled from unreconciled state returns is defensible statistical practice.
caseAgainst: The Ministry has not stopped producing the number. It gave it to the Standing Committee in January 2025 and let it be printed in August 2025; when an MP quoted those same two figures back in December 2025, the Minister declined to confirm his own department’s numbers. A statistic furnished to a committee and withheld from the House has not ceased to exist - it has ceased to be answerable for. The Union also receives the data as a condition of releasing Samagra Shiksha money through the Project Approval Board, so the federal argument reaches the sanctioning question but not the collection question. And the substitution is not neutral: UDISE+ is the one instrument that lacks the denominator, so the switch removes the possibility of the question being answered rather than improving the answer. The Committee had already recorded, in its 363rd Report, that because the funds are granted by the Union it is imperative for the Department to seek the data and maintain it centrally.
differentFactsNote: The Department is counting administrative competence - which government sanctions a post, which one recruits against it, and therefore which one holds the record - and the Committee is counting a fiscal relationship, that the Union transfers the money the posts are paid from and conditions the transfer on state returns it already receives. Both are correct and neither contradicts the other. What the record establishes is that the dispute is not about whether the Union can know the number: it produced the number for a decade and produced it again in January 2025.

title: RTE section 26's ten per cent vacancy ceiling, breached in the Union's own schools
summary: Section 26 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 requires the appointing authority for any school established, owned, controlled or substantially financed by the appropriate Government to ensure that teacher vacancies do not exceed ten per cent of sanctioned strength. Measured national rates are 14 to 15 per cent. In Kendriya Vidyalayas, where the appropriate Government is the Union itself, the rate rose from 13.2 per cent (August 2024) to 17.1 (December 2025); in Navodaya Vidyalayas it rose from 23.6 to 29.6 per cent over twelve months - the statutory ceiling breached by a factor of three.
whatHappened: The provision was not invoked. None of the four Rajya Sabha Standing Committee reports retrieved - the 363rd, 368th, 373rd and 376th - cites section 26. The Committee argues from adequacy and from 'the spirit of RTE Act' and does not reach for the binding numeric provision its own subject-matter statute contains. The Department's own compliance answer invokes a different measure entirely: 'the overall pupil-teacher ratio of the country is 25:1 across all levels, that is within the norms laid down under the RTE Act' - a national mean offered against a school-by-school duty. Meanwhile the Union filled the gap with contract staff rather than posts: KVS contract engagements rose from 3,260 (2020-21) to 7,909 (2025-26), about 15.7 per cent of sanctioned teaching strength against 8,618 vacant posts, and NVS contract teaching appointments rose 43 per cent from 2021 to 2025 while its vacancy rate rose with them.
caseFor: Vacancy is a flow, not a stock, and a ten per cent ceiling measured on a single date is close to unmeetable in a system of this size: retirements, resignations, promotions and new sanctions create posts continuously, and a recruitment cycle running through advertisement, examination, result, litigation and joining takes longer than the vacancies take to arise. The central institutions have not left classrooms empty - they engage contract teachers precisely so that, in NVS's own words, 'to protect the academic interest of students, teachers are being appointed on short term contract basis till the vacancies are filled on regular basis', so the teaching position on the ground is materially better than the vacancy rate implies. And KVS and NVS are the most transparent part of the system: their sanctioned, in-position and vacant figures are precise, dated and reported annually, which is exactly why the breach is visible here and invisible for the 99.8 per cent of schools the states run.
caseAgainst: Section 26 is not a target, an aspiration or a norm to be balanced against operational reality. It is a statutory duty, expressed as a number, owed by the appointing authority - and for Kendriya and Navodaya Vidyalayas the appointing authority is the Union, which has undivided control, its own recruitment machinery, its own budget and no federal excuse of any kind. It is breached at 1.7 times the ceiling in one and 3.0 times in the other, and the trend is worsening in both, across seventeen and twelve months respectively. The contract-staff answer concedes the point rather than rebutting it: contract engagement is rising in step with vacancies rather than in place of a recruitment cycle, KVS itself calls it a stop-gap arrangement for which 'specifying a fixed contract period is not possible', and it has been the arrangement for at least five years. The Committee's directive to fill these posts with regular teachers 'not later than 31st March, 2026' was, on the Committee's own figures as at 31 December 2025, not going to be met. And in fifteen years no report, no reply and no committee has cited the section: a binding numeric provision has sat unenforced in the governing statute while everyone argued about ratios.

title: The RTE untrained-teacher deadline: missed, retrospectively cured, and the outcome never published
summary: RTE section 23(2) gave in-service teachers without the prescribed minimum qualifications five years from commencement to acquire them, expiring 31 March 2015 unmet. The RTE (Amendment) Act 2017, passed more than two years after that deadline had lapsed and deemed to have come into force on 1 April 2015, inserted a second free-standing proviso giving a fresh four-year window to 31 March 2019. Around 14 lakh untrained teachers were registered on an 18-month distance diploma created for the purpose. No enrolled-to-appeared-to-passed-to-certified breakdown was ever published, and no count exists of teachers dismissed or still untrained on 1 April 2019.
claimAtLaunch: That this 'will be the last chance to acquire the requisite minimum qualifications and that any untrained teacher would not be allowed to continue in-service beyond 1st April 2019' - MHRD letter to all State and UT Education Secretaries, 3 August 2017, with the Minister stating publicly that there would be 'no further extension for this training programme after 31st March, 2019'.
whatHappened: The 2017 Act did not substitute or extend the original proviso; it INSERTED a second one, so the original five-year proviso remains on the statute book unamended with its 31 March 2015 deadline permanently unmet. On 22 September 2017 the NCTE relaxed its own recognition regulations to cut the distance-mode D.El.Ed. from two years to 18 months by subsuming the six-month internship, and recognised NIOS to deliver it - a duration the Supreme Court later recorded was set by the roughly 18 to 19 months remaining in the statutory window, not by the pedagogy. The programme opened 3 October 2017, registered 13,78,979 teachers, was budgeted at 453.62 crore - about 3,240 rupees per teacher - and ran four examination sittings to March 2019. The Ministry's Annual Report then recorded that 'around 14 lakh unqualified teachers were registered and were trained in the D.El.Ed. course... This is the largest initiative of its kind in the world.' The deadline was never statutorily extended again: section 23 has been amended once and only once. What happened instead is that the question migrated into seven and a half years of litigation about whether the qualification the Government itself created counted at all, resolved only in April 2025 and only conditionally.
caseFor: Roughly 14 lakh serving teachers who lacked the prescribed qualification were brought into a structured programme in eighteen months, delivered through 12,000 study centre coordinators, 54,000 resource persons, a national online platform and a dedicated broadcast channel - which is, as the Ministry says, plausibly the largest in-service teacher-training exercise ever attempted anywhere. The alternative to the amendment was dismissing a substantial fraction of India's primary teaching workforce on 1 April 2015 with no replacement supply, in a system already short of teachers; Parliament chose continuity of teaching over a cliff edge, and said so plainly in the Statement of Objects and Reasons, that states 'have not been able to continue the training process for in-service untrained teachers'. The deadline was genuinely not extended a third time. And the Supreme Court, in 2025, held the 18-month diploma valid at par with the two-year qualification for the teachers it was designed for.
caseAgainst: A statutory duty was missed and then legislatively regularised more than two years after the fact, with retrospective effect, by a Parliament that left the original unmet proviso standing and simply added another beside it. The qualification's duration was reverse-engineered to the residual window rather than to what it takes to train a teacher - the Court's own recital says so. And the state then declared the backlog cleared using a REGISTRATION number: 'registered and were trained' conflates the input with the output, and no enrolled-appeared-passed-certified breakdown exists in any source, although NIOS published semester results in May 2019 and plainly holds the data. Nor does any count exist, in either direction, of how many teachers were dismissed or remained untrained on 1 April 2019, after the Government had committed in writing that none would continue. Seven years later roughly one in eight primary teachers still lacks the prescribed qualification on the Ministry's own published figure, and on the statutorily operative definition it is closer to one in two. The credential itself was then adjudicated conditional: valid only for those in employment as on 10 August 2017, so holders who were not are being terminated in at least one state on that ground.

title: Devesh Sharma: B.Ed. removed as a primary-teaching qualification
summary: On 28 June 2018 the National Council for Teacher Education notified B.Ed. holders as eligible for primary (Classes I-V) teaching posts subject to a six-month bridge course. On 11 August 2023 the Supreme Court quashed and set aside that notification, holding from Article 21A that B.Ed. holders 'did not pass the basic professional threshold required for teaching students of the primary classes'. The published statistic 'professionally qualified teachers' consequently no longer corresponds to any legal status: as at 2026 at least four legally distinct populations are scored identically.
whatHappened: By a subsequent order of 8 April 2024 the Court declined to unseat B.Ed. holders already appointed and directed the NCTE to design a bridge course. The resulting six-month NIOS bridge course is live: eligibility runs to those appointed between 28 June 2018 and 11 August 2023, 'failure to complete the course within timeframe given by the concerned educational authorities will invalidate the appointment of such candidates', and it 'will not be valid for the teachers seeking subsequent employments as primary teachers' - it cures the individual appointment, not the credential. Registration windows remain open to 30 August 2026. Separately, in Kousik Das (4 April 2025) the Court held the 18-month distance D.El.Ed. valid at par with the two-year diploma, but only for teachers in employment as on 10 August 2017 who completed before 1 April 2019.
caseFor: The notification had a coherent purpose: India was short of teachers, B.Ed. is a full professional teacher-education degree taken by a large graduate population, and admitting them to primary posts subject to a bridge course widened a constrained supply without admitting untrained people. On any ordinary meaning of the words, a B.Ed. holder teaching Class III is professionally qualified - they are not an untrained person, and the Ministry's published statistic counting them as such is not a fabrication. The Court itself did not treat the appointments as void: it declined to unseat sitting appointees and directed a remediation route, which is a recognition that the disruption of removing them would fall on children.
caseAgainst: The measure was struck down in its entirety by the Supreme Court, five years after it was notified, on the ground that it lowered the professional threshold for the youngest children - the group whose foundational learning the government's own flagship mission identifies as the binding constraint. The consequence for measurement is that the Ministry's headline qualification statistic stopped meaning anything: 87.7 per cent of primary teachers are recorded as professionally qualified, but that counts people holding SOME recognised teaching credential, of whom an unquantified share hold one that does not authorise the class they teach. Computed on the statutorily operative definition from the same UDISE+ microdata, the figure is 45.72 per cent - a gap of roughly 42 points, which is the size of the B.Ed.-teaching-primary population and is a policy fact, not a measurement error. Eight years after the notification the remediation is still running, with registration open to August 2026 and non-completion invalidating the appointment, so a cohort of serving primary teachers holds employment conditional on a course they have not yet finished - and nobody has counted them.

title: RTE section 12(1)(c): the 25 per cent private-school quota
summary: Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act requires private unaided schools to reserve 25 per cent of entry-class seats for children from disadvantaged groups and weaker sections, with the state reimbursing a notified per-child cost. Central co-funding of that reimbursement began in 2014-15. By 2021-22 the Ministry reported 48.97 lakh children in schools for which reimbursement was claimed. On the Ministry's own count 19 of 36 States and UTs were admitting children under the provision as at April 2023 - roughly half the country has never operated it.
whatHappened: Central reimbursement runs through Samagra Shiksha at a state-notified per-child cost for Classes I-VIII, subject to a ceiling of 20 per cent of the state's approved Annual Work Plan and Budget, with states paying first and claiming afterwards. Approvals ran at 70.6 per cent of claims in FY2020-21 rising to 88.1 per cent in FY2024-25, a cumulative shortfall of 2,451.39 crore against claims of 11,856.67 crore. In December 2024, asked directly to name the states that had failed to implement the Act and why, the Ministry gave no list and did not answer, replying only that education is in the Concurrent List. In January 2026 the Supreme Court issued directions across the preparatory, application and post-admission stages and observed that 'all States and Union Territories have neither implemented the mandate of Section 12, nor established a portal dedicated to ensuring a transparent admission process'.
caseFor: The provision moved from close to nothing to a standing entitlement operating at scale: fill rates were 21.5 per cent in 2012-13 and 29.0 in 2013-14, and by 2021-22 nearly 49 lakh children were in private schools with their fees reimbursed. Central co-funding began in the first year of T1, extending a state obligation into a shared one where none had existed. The approval rate rose steadily from 70.6 to 88.1 per cent across five years, and the count of implementing jurisdictions rose from 17 to 19, with Manipur starting in 2024-25 after a Supreme Court notice. The scheme also survived a structural threat: SSA was subsumed into Samagra Shiksha in 2018-19 and the 12(1)(c) line survived the merger intact, still sanctioning and reimbursing through 2025-26.
caseAgainst: Sixteen years after enactment and twelve after central co-funding began, roughly half of India's jurisdictions have never operated the provision at all - and in December 2024 the Ministry, asked directly which ones and why, declined to answer. That refusal is itself a datum. Nor can anyone measure the shortfall, because the fill rate cannot be computed: no national series of seats notified against seats filled exists, the Ministry does not maintain one, and where the Ministry does use the word 'seats' the figure is demonstrably a lagged reimbursement headcount - for one state it equals exactly the previous year's approved reimbursement count for three consecutive years, producing a hundred per cent fill rate by construction. Two official-derived national series of children covered diverge by up to 1.95 million in the same year. The money is worse: 2,451 crore of state claims went unapproved, one state was approved a tenth of its claim in a year, and the Centre states plainly that its share is 'released to State/UTs based on approved funding pattern and not intervention wise' - so it does not know and cannot report how much reached schools. Upstream, the per-child cost norm that gates every claim has no national framework: asked twice, 22 months apart, whether it would standardise the calculation, the Ministry gave a word-for-word identical answer and the count of states that had revised their norm since 2014-15 did not move. And the entitlement is narrowed by construction: minority institutions are exempt entirely following Pramati, and pre-primary admissions - where many states actually admit - are outside central reimbursement altogether.

title: Karnataka's neighbourhood rule and the collapse of quota participation
summary: The Karnataka RTE (Amendment) Rules 2018, gazetted 30 January 2019, provided that admission under section 12(1)(c) would be available only where there is no government or aided school in the defined neighbourhood offering the relevant class. Private schools admitting children under the provision in Karnataka fell from 12,165 (2018-19) to 219 (2019-20) - a 98.2 per cent collapse in one year, against a national pattern of flat or rising participation. The Karnataka High Court upheld the rule on 31 May 2019.
whatHappened: Participation stayed collapsed: 221 schools in 2020-21. Every other large state moved the other way or held flat over the same two years - Rajasthan 27,013 to 28,358, Madhya Pradesh 22,964 to 26,976, Uttar Pradesh 13,936 to 20,719, Gujarat 7,775 to 9,775, Maharashtra 8,166 to 9,195. Karnataka's seat count is reported at 17,718 for 2019-20 with 4,701 admissions. The state has continued to claim and receive central reimbursement of almost exactly 200 crore every year since - the 20-per-cent-of-budget ceiling binding rather than demand - against a stock of children admitted in earlier years.
caseFor: The rule is a defensible reading of the Act's own architecture. Section 12(1)(c) sits inside a statute built on the neighbourhood school: the child's right is to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school, and the private-school quota was designed to reach children for whom no such school was available. Where a government or aided school exists in the neighbourhood, the state's position was that the child's entitlement is already met and public money is better spent on that school than on reimbursing a private one. The Karnataka High Court examined the amendment and upheld it. The fiscal logic is real too: reimbursement is capped at 20 per cent of the state's education budget, so every rupee reimbursed to a private school is a rupee unavailable to the government system that teaches the overwhelming majority of children - and Karnataka's government schools were simultaneously among those with the worst measured learning outcomes.
caseAgainst: A 98.2 per cent fall in one year is not a refinement of a provision; it is its nullification by administrative rule, in a state where 12,165 private schools had been admitting children under it the year before. The entitlement in section 12(1)(c) is a parent's choice conferred by central statute, not a residual to be allocated by the state where it judges public provision inadequate - and the practical effect is that the children the provision exists for, who by definition live where government schools are, lost access to it precisely because a government school was nearby. Nothing in the rule improved the government school in the neighbourhood; it only closed the alternative. And the national pattern removes the innocent explanations: no other state saw anything comparable in the same years, so this was a rule change and not a demand shift, a pandemic effect, or a reporting artefact. The state continued to draw the full 200-crore reimbursement afterwards, so the money did not follow the children out.

title: NEP 2020's three-language formula and Tamil Nadu's refusal
summary: NEP 2020 paragraph 4.13 retains the three-language formula while removing every named language from it: 'no language will be imposed on any State', the three being 'the choices of States, regions, and of course the students themselves, so long as at least two of the three languages are native to India'. Tamil Nadu, whose Assembly resolved on 23 January 1968 'that the Three-Language Formula shall be scrapped', has refused to implement it. The Union's own position, stated in Parliament in March 2026, is that 'Tamil Nadu is not implementing it in its entirety'.
whatHappened: The word 'Hindi' appears nowhere in NEP's language chapter. Sanskrit is named twice as an option in the three-language formula. The Union restated paragraph 4.13 verbatim in at least five parliamentary answers and added that the modalities are for states to decide, education being in the Concurrent List. Tamil Nadu released its own State Education Policy on 8 August 2025, based on a committee report submitted 1 July 2024, retaining the two-language formula. The single most important empirical datum arrived from elsewhere: Maharashtra, a state that adopted NEP in full, issued Government Resolutions in April and June 2025 introducing Hindi as the third language from Class 1, and withdrew both on 29 June 2025 after sustained opposition. Karnataka - a state with no anti-Hindi tradition comparable to Tamil Nadu's, which implemented the three-language formula for decades - moved to a two-language formula in its own 2025 State Education Policy.
caseFor: The Union's case is textual and it is accurate. NEP 2020 names no language at all: 'Hindi' does not occur in the language chapter, the choice is expressly assigned to states, regions and students, and the only constraint is that two of the three be native to India. That is a real and substantive change from 1968, which named Hindi and made it compulsory in non-Hindi states, and from the 1992 Programme of Action, which provided 100 per cent central assistance for appointing Hindi teachers in non-Hindi states. The anti-imposition sentence has no antecedent in either earlier policy. NEP is a policy, not a statute; no Act of Parliament enacts it; and the Supreme Court confirmed in May 2025 that it 'cannot directly compel a state to adopt a policy like the National Education Policy, 2020'. Thirty-three of 36 States and UTs have signed the implementation memorandum. And the three-language count itself is not a 2020 innovation - it is the residue of a 1968 national consensus that Tamil Nadu rejected then and rejects now.
caseAgainst: Tamil Nadu's objection is to the cardinality, not the content, and on that the Union does not engage. Paragraph 4.13's opening clause is affirmative - the formula 'will continue to be implemented' - and the flexibility clause modifies WHICH languages, not HOW MANY; the curriculum framework operationalises it as three languages with proficiency in the third targeted by age 14. The arithmetic then follows from the Union's own text without any empirical claim: in a Tamil-and-English school the existing two are Tamil, which is native to India, and English, which is not, so the mandatory third cannot be a foreign language and must be an Indian language other than Tamil - and the only language NEP nominates for that slot anywhere in its 66 pages is Sanskrit. 'No language will be imposed' therefore delivers a choice among Indian languages other than Tamil, not a choice that includes no third language. The supply argument is conceded by NEP itself: paragraph 4.12 proposes that states 'enter into bilateral agreements to hire teachers in large numbers from each other, to satisfy the three-language formula', which is a policy admitting that local supply of non-Hindi, non-Sanskrit Indian-language teachers is inadequate. History runs the same way: the 1992 Programme of Action recorded that 'no provision exists for the teaching of South Indian languages in the Hindi speaking States' and that some states substituted a classical language for a modern Indian one. NEP 2020 removed the 1968 corrective - 'preferably one of the southern languages' in Hindi states - along with everything else language-specific, while keeping the obligation, so the burden asymmetry the corrective existed to close is now unaddressed in the text. And Maharashtra settles what the flexible formula converts into in practice: a state that adopted NEP in full, when it operationalised the formula, selected Hindi from Class 1.

title: Samagra Shiksha funds withheld from states that have not adopted NEP 2020
summary: Tamil Nadu, Kerala and West Bengal received nil central Samagra Shiksha release in FY2024-25, against 1,876.16, 141.66 and 311.29 crore respectively the year before. All three are the three States that have not signed the PM-SHRI memorandum of understanding; 33 of 36 States and UTs have. The Union's stated position is that 'implementation of Samagra Shiksha is implementation of NEP, 2020' and that Tamil Nadu 'has not agreed to implement NEP, 2020 in its entirety'. Nothing in NEP 2020 authorises the conditionality; the linkage runs through the PM-SHRI memorandum and the 2021 realignment of Samagra Shiksha to the policy.
whatHappened: Tamil Nadu was allocated 2,151.59 crore of central share for FY2024-25 and released 362.81 crore of it, a year late in FY2025-26; for FY2025-26 it was allocated 1,896.42 crore and had received 175.58 crore as at 5 March 2026. The Department stated that 'keeping in view the larger perspective as well as educational needs of the children of Tamil Nadu, DoSEL decided to release admissible Central share of the RTE Entitlements component' - so the entitlement component was carved out and released while the rest was not. Tamil Nadu filed an original suit in the Supreme Court over the withheld funds; the Court declined an urgent hearing. In a separate matter on 9 May 2025 the Court dismissed a petition seeking to compel the three states to implement NEP, holding that it 'cannot directly compel a state to adopt a policy like the National Education Policy, 2020', while noting it could intervene if a state's action or inaction violated fundamental or other legal rights.
caseFor: Samagra Shiksha is a centrally sponsored scheme, not an unconditional transfer, and it was explicitly revamped in 2021 to align with NEP 2020. A state that declines to implement the scheme as designed is declining the scheme, and the Union's obligation runs to the scheme's terms rather than to a state's preferred variant of it. Conditionality on scheme design is ordinary and is how every centrally sponsored scheme in India works. The Union also did not withhold indiscriminately: it carved out and released the RTE Entitlements component to Tamil Nadu on the express ground of the educational needs of children, so the statutory entitlements were protected while the policy-linked components were not. And the Supreme Court, asked to intervene from the other direction, declined to compel the states - which confirms that the choice is genuinely the states' and that they are exercising it with the fiscal consequence that follows.
caseAgainst: Education is in the Concurrent List, the Union says so in every parliamentary answer on this subject, and NEP 2020 is a Cabinet-approved policy that no Act of Parliament enacts - there is no legal instrument compelling a state to adopt it, and the Supreme Court has said so. What cannot be achieved by law is being achieved by money: three states received nil against allocations of thousands of crores, and the equation 'implementation of Samagra Shiksha is implementation of NEP 2020' is a policy-design assertion by the Department, not a claim about the NEP text or about any statute. The scale is the point: 2,151.59 crore allocated to Tamil Nadu and 362.81 released, a year late, and 175.58 of 1,896.42 the following year - against a state school system serving crores of children who are not party to the disagreement. The carve-out concedes the principle: if children's educational needs justify releasing the RTE component, the same needs are attached to the components withheld. And the conditionality runs through a memorandum for a scheme covering a few thousand schools, PM-SHRI, whose signature has become the gate for the main school-education transfer.

title: Public education spending: two official numerators moving in opposite directions
summary: The Ministry of Education publishes two totals for public education spending side by side, in one table, for the same year. For FY2021-22 they are 2.75 and 4.12 per cent of GDP. Across FY2013-14 to FY2021-22 the broad basis rises from 3.84 to 4.12 per cent and the narrow basis falls from 2.97 to 2.75. Same budgets, opposite direction, purely from numerator choice. The series stops at FY2021-22: no edition covering FY2022-23 or later has been published, and T3 has zero observations.
claimAtLaunch: A standing commitment, restated in NEP 2020 and in Parliament, to 'increase the public investment in Education sector to reach 6% of GDP at the earliest'.
whatHappened: Parliament is briefed on the broad number - the Standing Committee's 363rd Report reproduces the broad series verbatim - and the 6 per cent target is invoked against it, so the gap to target is 1.9 points or 3.3 points depending on a definitional choice that is never stated when the target is invoked. The Ministry of Education is 39 per cent of what the 4.12 per cent headline calls education; the rest is training plus the education spending of roughly 44 other ministries. States carry about three-quarters of the money throughout. The Centre's own education-department spending fell from 0.64 to 0.40 per cent of GDP across the same window, the lowest in the twenty-two-year table, and real Union education spending in FY2024-25 was barely above FY2013-14 - eleven years of near-zero real growth. Economic Survey 2025-26 dropped the education-share-of-GDP table entirely.
caseFor: On the headline measure the government reports and Parliament is briefed on, education spending rose across the transition: 3.84 per cent of GDP in FY2013-14 to a peak of 4.24 in FY2016-17 and 4.12 in FY2021-22, against a UPA-2 average of 3.87. The broad definition is not a trick - it is the government's own long-standing accounting convention, unchanged in construction across editions, and its rationale is defensible: mid-day-meal nutrition, anganwadi provision, medical and agricultural education, scientific research and training are education spending by any reasonable account, and the Economic Survey's own note documents exactly what is swept in. And the structure of the shortfall is not the Union's alone to fix: states carry three-quarters of the money, so a Union-budget-only story about Indian education spending is a story about a quarter of it.
caseAgainst: On the measure most readers mean by education spending - what education departments actually spend - the share fell every single year of T1, from 2.97 per cent in FY2013-14 to a twenty-two-year minimum of 2.61 in FY2018-19, and stood at 2.75 in the last published year, below the 3.22 per cent of FY2010-11. The gap between the two measures is not a constant that can be reasoned around: it roughly tripled across the table, from 0.52 points in FY2004-05 to 1.46 in FY2016-17, and other departments' share of the total rose from 15.9 to 33.3 per cent - so the headline is increasingly driven by non-education ministries. And the improvement itself is unexplained: other-departments education spending grew 41.7 then 49.0 per cent across FY2013-14 and FY2014-15, roughly doubling in two years, exactly at the political transition, against 11.4 and 8.4 per cent for education departments - and no retrieved document accounts for it. Both terminal points are Budget Estimates, which revise down by about 0.35 points to Actual on the only year where all three stages exist, and the Union underspent its own budget in 13 of 16 completed years. The pre-2011-12 rows sit on a spliced GDP denominator that inflates the UPA years by 0.16 to 0.29 points with no note in the source. And the series has simply stopped: a twenty-five-year annual statistical publication has produced nothing covering FY2022-23 onward, so the current term cannot be assessed on it at all.

title: AISHE ceases to be a timely series
summary: The All India Survey on Higher Education, which through the mid-2010s carried a cover year one year after its survey year, published AISHE 2019-20 eighteen months after its reference date, 2020-21 and 2021-22 at twenty-five months each, and then nothing for twenty-nine months. AISHE 2022-23 and 2023-24 were released together on 8 July 2026, the former three years and six months after its own reference date. AISHE 2024-25 remains unpublished.
whatHappened: The lag is not a collection problem: the 2022-23 report states 'The Survey was held between 18th November, 2022 till March, 2024', so collection closed in March 2024 and the report appeared 28 months later - the binding constraint sits between scrutiny and publication. The consequence is demonstrated rather than inferred. Economic Survey 2025-26 quoted an AISHE 2022-23 higher-education gross enrolment ratio of 29.5 while the AISHE 2022-23 report was still unpublished, and the same Survey's statistical appendix - unable to cite an unpublished report - fell back on AISHE 2021-22 and printed 28.4. Two figures for the same quantity in one document, because one arm of government had the number and another could not cite it.
caseFor: The survey continued to be conducted throughout and eventually published, with no gap in the data itself: every reference year from 2019-20 to 2023-24 exists and is in the public domain, and the 2022-23 and 2023-24 releases restored the sequence. Scrutiny takes time in a voluntary self-reported survey covering roughly 70,000 institutions where response is incomplete and non-responders' returns have to be handled; publishing a bad number quickly would be worse than a good number late. The Ministry also published the restated 2011-Census-basis GER series openly, disclosing a denominator change that lowered its own headline figure by about 1.5 points - which is not the behaviour of a body managing its numbers.
caseAgainst: A statistic published three and a half years after its reference date is not a statistic for any decision it was collected to inform: district and institution planning for 2022-23 was over before the 2022-23 data existed. The lag is era-shaped - under a year in the mid-2010s, opening in T2 and reaching its maximum in T3 - so this is a deterioration, not a constant condition. Publishing two reference years on one day compounds it: the superseded year enters the record already paired with its successor, exactly as happened with school enrolment. And the Economic Survey episode shows the cost precisely: the number existed in government hands and was used in the government's flagship economic document months before the report containing it was released, so the delay is in publication and not in production - the strongest available form of a not-published finding, because producibility is demonstrated rather than inferred. Meanwhile the survey's own scheme authority runs only to 2025-26 and no document extending it was retrieved, and the first placement module - the survey's first attempt at an outcome measure in fourteen years - sits inside the unpublished 2024-25 round.

title: Higher education: enrolment growth decelerates and the denominator does half the work
summary: On the restated 2011-Census-projection basis, higher-education gross enrolment among 18-23 year olds rose from 21.2 per cent (2011-12) to 30.0 (2023-24), with female GER crossing above male in 2017-18 and staying above for seven consecutive years. Enrolment rose 31.5 per cent over the decade. But growth has decelerated sharply to 0.8 per cent in 2023-24, undergraduate enrolment fell in absolute terms that year, and roughly half of the most recent GER gain is the projected 18-23 population shrinking rather than additional students.
whatHappened: The projected denominator fell 1,282,000 between 2022 and 2023; holding it at its 2022 value the 2023-24 GER would be 29.77 rather than 30.0. Male GER was flat at 28.9 in both years, so all of the increase is female enrolment plus the shrinking denominator. Beneath the aggregate, the traditional core contracted: B.A. fell from 93.8 to 89.6 lakh, B.Sc. from 46.3 to 44.7 lakh and B.Com. from 37.4 to 34.1 lakh, with the total held up by engineering, computer applications, nursing, pharmacy, diploma and doctoral programmes. Central universities went from 48 to 55 across the same window while state private universities went from 327 to 464 - the fastest-growing category by far. The funding model changed too: infrastructure capital that was formerly a grant is now a loan carried on institutions' books, with roughly 1,693 crore of debt service budgeted in BE FY2025-26 from a standing start in FY2019-20.
caseFor: Nearly nine percentage points of gross enrolment ratio in twelve years is a large expansion by any international standard, and 1.08 crore additional students is a bigger absolute increase than most countries' entire higher-education systems. The gains are distributionally the right shape: SC GER rose from 15.3 to 27.8 and ST from 11.2 to 22.8, both faster than the national rate, and female GER overtook male in 2017-18 and has stayed above ever since - a reversal of the oldest gap in Indian higher education. Institutional supply expanded to match, with universities roughly doubling and colleges rising by nearly 13,000. And the denominator restatement, which lowered the headline by about 1.5 points, was disclosed by the survey itself rather than discovered.
caseAgainst: The headline flatters on both sides of the ratio. Roughly half the most recent gain is the 18-23 cohort contracting, not students arriving - and as that cohort continues to shrink, GER will keep rising on flat enrolment, so the 50-per-cent-by-2035 target becomes progressively easier to hit without teaching anyone. The whole denominator rests on a population projection whose census base is now fifteen years old. On the numerator, growth has collapsed to 0.8 per cent and undergraduate enrolment fell in absolute terms in 2023-24 - the arts, science and commerce core of Indian higher education contracted, and this is invisible in the headline. The numerator is also not a measurement but a voluntary self-reported administrative return: the Ministry's own words are that 'participation in AISHE is voluntary, and the data is self-reported by the HEIs', the advertised 90-plus per cent participation is post-pooling rather than actual response, and roughly 31 per cent of standalone institutions in the 2023-24 figures carry data one to two years old. And the whole expansion is measured only at entry: India has no published higher-education dropout, retention or completion rate at all - an exhaustive search of every AISHE report from 2014-15 to 2023-24 returns zero occurrences of the terms - so nobody knows what share of the 1.08 crore additional entrants finished anything.

title: Literacy: the last complete enumeration is 2011
summary: Census 2021 was never fielded. The intent notification of 16 June 2025 supersedes the 2019 notification and sets Census 2027 with a reference date of 1 March 2027. Literacy is a Population Enumeration question, and Population Enumeration is not yet notified; the gazette notification defining the Census 2027 literacy question does not yet exist. India's last complete enumeration of literacy is 2011, at 72.98 per cent - and the figure in general circulation is the provisional 74.04.
whatHappened: Literacy has continued to be measured on a sample basis throughout: NSS 75th Round put it at 77.7 per cent for 2017-18 and PLFS at 81.1 per cent for calendar 2025, both at the Census's own 7-plus frame and on essentially the Census definition. What a sample cannot do is what is missing: sub-district granularity, so every district and block literacy plan and all ULLAS targeting runs on 2011 geography; small-group disaggregation by caste, tribe, religion and language at fine geography; and population denominators, since surveys give rates while the Census gives the counts of illiterate persons that programmes are sized against. By publication this will be a sixteen-to-eighteen-year interval, the longest since the Indian census series began in 1881. Economic Survey 2025-26, published in January 2026, still describes India's population and its literacy as of 2011.
caseFor: The postponement has a stated and adequate cause: preparations for the first phase were complete and field work was scheduled to begin on 1 April 2020 when the pandemic intervened, and enumerating 1.4 billion people door to door was not available in 2020 or 2021. The legal trace is unambiguous and public - the 2019 notification was formally superseded, not quietly abandoned - and the replacement is under way rather than promised: House Listing Operations were in month five of six on 1 August 2026, the second-phase pre-test was completed in July 2026, and the exercise adds self-enumeration for the first time. Meanwhile India did not stop measuring literacy: PLFS publishes an annual rate on the Census's own definition and frame, most recently for calendar 2025, so the country has a current national number and a recent one at state level.
caseAgainst: India will go at least sixteen years between complete enumerations of its own population, the longest gap in 146 years, and the consequences compound across the entire instrument rather than sitting in one indicator: every post-2011 per-capita and rate-based figure in Indian official statistics now rests on projections, including the school gross enrolment ratios, the higher-education gross enrolment ratio and ASER's own village sampling frame. The specific loss in literacy is granularity, and it is the granularity that programmes are built on: block-level targeting for the national literacy mission runs on a geography that is fifteen years out of date. The caste enumeration announced alongside Census 2027 has no defining instrument yet - the intent notification does not mention caste at all, and the only question notification issued so far covers the first phase's 33 items, whose social-category question is the same three-way split as 2011. And the sample substitute is weaker than it looks: every official instrument measures literacy by asking, not testing - the enumerator poses the question to a household informant, often about other members, and no reading or writing task is administered at any point, so a literate person is a person someone said was literate. Where both methods have been run on the same respondents the gap was 5.6 points, and that is a floor.

title: Single-teacher schools and the ratio norm that permits them
summary: RTE section 25 required the pupil-teacher ratio in the Act's Schedule to be maintained 'in each school' within three years of commencement, that is by 31 March 2013. Thirteen years later about one lakh schools have a single teacher - 104,125 in FY2024-25, 7.08 per cent of all schools, falling to about 100,843 in FY2025-26 - while the Department answers the school-level duty with a national mean of 25:1. Both are true at once because the norm is a ratio and not a coverage rule.
whatHappened: The Act does not contain the figure 30:1 that everyone cites, including the Standing Committee about its own governing statute. The Schedule prescribes a staffing SLAB for Classes I-V - two teachers up to sixty children, three up to ninety, rising to a ceiling of 40:1 above two hundred - and its only explicit ratio is 35:1 for Classes VI-VIII. On that reading the binding norm for a small primary school is two teachers, so every single-teacher school is in breach of the Schedule independently of any ratio, and no official document retrieved applies that test. The distributional indicator that would show compliance was published annually by the predecessor system through 2015-16 - one in four primary schools above the norm in its final year - and has never been published since, although the current system holds school-level enrolment and teacher counts for every school. The single computation of it since is a university centre's, from 2021-22 microdata: 24 per cent of all schools above 35:1, 81 per cent of them rural, with 70 per cent of government schools in Bihar and 50 per cent in Delhi carrying a teacher requirement.
caseFor: The count is falling and the direction has been sustained: single-teacher schools went from 118,190 (FY2022-23) to about 100,843 (FY2025-26), a 15 per cent reduction in three years, and enrolment in them fell faster still, from 47.4 lakh to 29.1 lakh. National pupil-teacher ratios are inside every norm at every level and improving, the total teaching workforce crossed one crore for the first time, and the deployment problem is genuinely a state function in a system where the Union runs 0.2 per cent of schools. Many single-teacher schools also exist for a defensible reason: they are small, remote and hilly, and the alternative to a one-teacher school in such a habitation is no school - which is why the access ratio for primary schooling stands at 97.8 per cent of habitations.
caseAgainst: A statutory duty owed school by school, with a deadline of 31 March 2013, is unmet in about a lakh schools thirteen years later, and the state answers it with a national average - a category error, since a mean of 25:1 is consistent with any distribution, including this one. The Committee states the mechanism plainly: a ratio norm 'took the focus away from the importance of having one teacher per grade', and is satisfiable by a small school with one teacher and thirty children spread across five grades. That is not a hypothetical: 91 per cent of single-teacher schools are primary schools, two-thirds of Standard I and II classrooms are multigrade, and the Committee notes that a single teacher's illness closes the school. The supply explanation does not hold everywhere either - the states with the highest shares include several with adequate supply of qualified teachers, which makes it a deployment failure rather than a shortage. And the improvement is partly not one: single-teacher schools fell by about 17,000 across three years while the total school stock fell by roughly 5,000 and zero-enrolment schools by 4,631, so part of the reduction is closure and consolidation - a split no source decomposes, while the Ministry attributes the whole of it to 'conscious and meaningful governmental interventions'. Finally the indicator itself did not exist in the national system before FY2022-23, so its first published value sits exactly on the reporting-base shift with a six-year hole behind it covering most of T1.

title: Contract teaching: collected for every teacher, published for none
summary: The school data capture format records, for every one of the roughly 1.01 crore individual teacher records in India, a field 'Nature of Appointment: 1-Regular, 2-Contract, 3-Part-Time/Guest', identically worded in the 2022-23 and 2025-26 editions. No UDISE+ report, press release, Economic Survey chapter or parliamentary reply publishes the national regular-versus-non-regular share. The only national estimate that exists was produced by a university centre for the UNESCO Teacher Task Force: 11.1 per cent of state-government-school teachers were contractual in 2021-22, and 16 per cent at primary level.
whatHappened: The Standing Committee asked for 'the details of appointments of permanent and ad-hoc/contractual teachers, separately' state-wise and year-wise, and received the same Concurrent-List reply that covers vacancies. Where the Union runs the schools itself the series does exist, and it shows the practice hardening: Kendriya Vidyalaya contract engagements rose from 3,260 (2020-21) to 7,909 (2025-26), about 15.7 per cent of sanctioned teaching strength, and Navodaya Vidyalaya contract teaching appointments rose 43 per cent from 2021 to 2025 - in both cases rising in step with vacancies rather than in place of a recruitment cycle, with KVS calling it 'a stop-gap arrangement' for which 'specifying a fixed contract period is not possible'.
caseFor: The measured national share is not high and is falling: 11.1 per cent of government-school teachers in 2021-22, down from about 13 per cent in 2013-14, with part-time teachers at 1 per cent nationally. Contract engagement in the Union's own schools is explicitly protective in intent - 'to protect the academic interest of students, teachers are being appointed on short term contract basis till the vacancies are filled on regular basis' - and the alternative to a contract teacher against a vacant post is an empty classroom. On publication, the Union's position is the constitutional one it applies consistently: recruitment and service conditions are state functions, the terms on which a state employs its own teachers are the state's to define and report, and a national aggregate of a field that means different things in different states would be a false precision - a point the independent computation itself concedes, noting that the definitions 'vary contextually, from state to state as well as between government and non-government/private managements'.
caseAgainst: The field exists, is mandatory, and is filled for every teacher in the country: this is not data the Union lacks, it is data the Union declines to aggregate. The distinction matters because it is the whole of the finding - the same Concurrent-List answer that covers vacancies covers employment terms, and in both cases the boundary is not what the Union can know but what it chooses to say. What the one independent computation shows is exactly why it matters: 90 per cent of contractual teachers are rural, 16 per cent of government primary teachers are contractual against 11 per cent overall, and the contract tier is more female than the regular tier at every level of aggregation - 55 per cent women against 44 per cent of the government workforce, and 80 per cent in aided primary schools. The apparent decline from 13 to 11 per cent is not a decline: the paper producing it says the fall is substantially reclassification, with several states extending contracts to retirement age so the same teachers re-code from contract to regular while remaining on lower salaries and outside government-servant status - 'invisible contract, quasi-regular teachers'. And the disaggregation that would show the consequence was dropped: the predecessor system published the trained share of contractual teachers separately, at 54 to 67 per cent against 79 to 82 for regular teachers, and its successor collects both fields and publishes neither cross-tab. The Committee's own reading is blunter still: regular recruitment 'has almost been stopped', the dual system 'creates a system of different pay for equal work', contractual appointment 'undermines the Constitutional provision reservation in Government jobs', and a commitment to end the practice present in the 2019 draft policy was absent from the 2020 final one.

title: The West Bengal teacher-recruitment panel annulled, and the anti-cheating law that does not reach it
summary: On 3 April 2025 the Supreme Court upheld the Calcutta High Court's judgment of 22 April 2024 setting aside en bloc the entire 2016 selection process of the West Bengal Central School Service Commission for Assistant Teachers of Classes IX-X and XI-XII and for non-teaching Group C and Group D staff. Six weeks before the High Court ruled, Parliament had enacted the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act 2024, whose Schedule does not cover any state school service commission, state public service commission, state teacher eligibility test or state teacher recruitment board.
whatHappened: The findings of fact the Court adopted are why segregating tainted from untainted candidates was unavailable: OMR sheets had been destroyed by the Commission's own executive decision of 22 July 2019 without scanned mirror images being preserved; the Commission had supplied purportedly scanned OMR sheets to information applicants from 2018 to 2023 although the investigating agency found none on its server; appointments exceeded declared vacancies in all four categories; appointments were given to persons not on the panel, to persons who submitted blank OMR sheets, and after the panel had expired; the merit list with candidates' marks was never published; the total beneficiaries of the illegalities remain unidentified; and the Commission had applied to create supernumerary posts to accommodate the illegal appointees. The Court's own line of authority requires every effort to segregate and holds en bloc cancellation incompatible with law where segregation is possible - so the remedy fell on candidates the Court did not find to have done anything wrong, and it directed that they may re-sit with age relaxation. The Act’s Schedule names six authorities: the Union Public Service Commission, the Staff Selection Commission, the Railway Recruitment Boards, the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, Ministries or Departments of the Central Government for recruitment of their own staff, and the National Testing Agency. Coverage therefore follows the conducting authority, not the employer - so a teacher-recruitment examination conducted by NTA for Kendriya Vidyalayas falls inside the Act while the Central Teacher Eligibility Test, conducted by CBSE for the same schools, falls outside it. No state school service commission, no state public service commission, no state teacher eligibility test and no state teacher recruitment board is listed, and the Act’s own Statement of Objects and Reasons says it "shall serve as a model draft for States to adopt at their discretion". Of the teacher-examination failures in this period - West Bengal 2016, Bihar TRE-3, UPTET 2021, REET 2021, the Rajasthan Senior Teacher paper of December 2022, Maharashtra TET 2018 and 2020, Haryana HTET 2015, Gujarat TAT 2018 and Odisha OTET 2019 - the central Act would have reached none.
caseFor: The system worked, slowly and at cost, but it worked: a fraudulent recruitment was investigated, litigated through two courts, and annulled, with a fresh selection process ordered and relief for candidates who had done nothing wrong. That is the constitutional machinery functioning against a state government, and the Supreme Court modified the High Court's directions rather than rubber-stamping them. On the central law, the exclusion of state recruitment is not an oversight but the constitutional position stated openly in the Statement of Objects and Reasons: the Bill 'shall serve as a model draft for States to adopt at their discretion. This would aid States in preventing the criminal elements from disrupting conduct of their State level public examinations.' Public examinations conducted by state bodies are for states to police, and the Union legislated for the sphere it controls.
caseAgainst: An entire year's teacher recruitment for the secondary and higher-secondary schools of a large state was voided nine years after it was held, and the reason segregation was impossible is that the recruiting authority destroyed the evidence by its own executive decision - so the remedy necessarily punished the innocent along with the rest, and the posts returned to the vacancy pool that the same state's schools were already short against. The Union's answer to examination fraud, enacted six weeks before the High Court judgment and fourteen months before the Supreme Court's, does not reach it: the Schedule covers the Union Public Service Commission, the Staff Selection Commission, railway recruitment boards, banking personnel selection, central ministries recruiting their own staff, and the National Testing Agency - and no state body, not even the board that conducts the central teacher eligibility test. The Act therefore reaches teacher recruitment only where the Union is itself the recruiter, which is the 0.2 per cent of schools it runs. That is the same federal boundary that prevents the Union from counting teacher vacancies reappearing as a gap in enforcement: the largest teacher-recruitment fraud in Indian history was a state process, and the national law was written to leave state processes to state discretion.
