unmeasured.why: The central Act’s Schedule names six conducting authorities and excludes every state recruitment and eligibility body, and CBSE with them, so no national reporting obligation attaches to state teacher recruitment examinations and no national series of cancellations, leaks or annulments exists. Three of the five state anti-paper-leak Acts - Haryana 2021, Uttarakhand 2023, Jharkhand 2023 - were drafted around the hiring examination and do not reach the licensing examination either; only Uttar Pradesh 2024, by writing "either qualifying or competitive" into its definition, and Gujarat 2023, by naming the State Examination Board in its Schedule, do. This is a coverage absence rather than a data absence, and it is recorded because it explains why the vacancy absence persists: the same federal boundary runs through both.

title: Private schooling plateaus while the government school stock falls
summary: The share of rural children aged 6-14 in private school rose steeply through the UPA years, from 18.7 per cent (2006) to 30.8 (2014), and then stopped: 30.6 in 2016, 30.9 in 2018, 25.1 in the COVID trough of 2022 and 30.6 in 2024. The privatisation of rural schooling stopped in 2014 and has never resumed. Over the same period the number of government schools fell from 1,107,101 (FY2014-15) to 1,005,245 (FY2025-26), a net decline of 101,856 or about 9.2 per cent, while private schools rose 18.5 per cent.
whatHappened: The COVID swing and its reversal are corroborated independently from both sides - the household survey and the administrative universe agree in direction on the one stretch where both are clean, with government enrolment up 8.1 million and private down 5.6 million across FY2020-21 to FY2021-22. ASER's reading of the reversal is that the shift into government schools was driven 'more by necessity rather than choice'. The largest single-year fall in the government school stock, 51,177 schools in FY2019-20, predates the enrolment re-basing and is therefore a separate phenomenon, largely one state. Asked twice, in February 2025 and February 2026, for the number of schools closed or merged year-wise and state-wise, the Ministry declined both times on the ground that 'the opening, closing and rationalisation of schools are within the purview of respective State Government and UT Administration', and answered instead with access and efficiency measures.
caseFor: A plateau in private share after a decade of steep growth is a reasonable reading of a government system that stopped losing ground: government share among rural 6-14s was 64.9 per cent in 2014 and 66.8 in 2024, higher than at the start of the period, and government-school learning outcomes improved materially in 2024 while private ones did not recover to 2018. School consolidation has a real rationale, and the access data supports it: the gross access ratio for a primary school within norm stands at 97.8 per cent of habitations and for higher secondary rose from 65.1 to 95.0 per cent across the same window, so the network reached further while the stock shrank. Merging two schools of twenty children into one of forty is a defensible answer to a demographic reality rather than a withdrawal.
caseAgainst: The published series is a stock and the state does not publish the flow, so nobody can say how many schools were closed as against merged, or how many children had to travel further. The widely circulated 'schools closed' figure is a stock difference that nets closures against openings, and the Ministry's Concurrent-List answer is contradicted by its own system: it operates a school-level database with a unique code per school from which closures and mergers are directly derivable, and it does publish flow-type counts for zero-enrolment and single-teacher schools over exactly the same years. Nor does consolidation appear to be working on the ground it claims: government primary schools with fewer than sixty children enrolled rose from 44.0 per cent (2022) to 52.1 (2024), so the stock is becoming more thinly populated, not less, and two-thirds of Standard I and II classrooms are multigrade. The efficiency answer also sits awkwardly beside the same reply's own disclosures: 0.3 per cent of government schools running without buildings, 12.0 per cent in dilapidated blocks and 13.4 per cent of primary schools with a single teacher.
